passage:
Dear Imran,

Thank you for not laughing when I told you on Sunday. I had been checking my crush's profile every few minutes: during physics, at dinner, at midnight. Last week's test came back with silly mistakes, and I didn't want to admit that a person I barely talk to was taking over my whole head. So I have logged out of the app on my phone and I look once at night, briefly. I also started the model for the science exhibition. The glue and cardboard fill the space that all the thinking used to. It hasn't gone away, but it is quieter. Could you ask me on Friday how it's going?

Kavitha

qa.q: What had Kavitha been checking every few minutes?
qa.a: Kavitha had been checking a crush's profile every few minutes.

qa.q: What worried Kavitha about the thoughts, and what showed it?
qa.a: Kavitha was worried and a little embarrassed that the thoughts were crowding out study, shown by the silly mistakes on last week's test.

qa.q: What else could Kavitha do if the thoughts stay strong, and why?
qa.a: Kavitha could talk to a parent or the school counsellor as well, because more support helps when a worry keeps taking over.

qa.q: How might Imran feel on reading the letter?
qa.a: Imran likely feels trusted and glad to help, especially with a request to ask again on Friday.

grounding: Noticing that thoughts about the crush crowd out study, the student limits checking online, tells a trusted person, and puts the energy into a project, which lowers the intensity.

passage: I'm Asif, and I'll be honest: last autumn I was a bit gone. I liked Arohi from the other section, and I checked her posts maybe thirty times a day. I'd open my Physics book and end up refreshing her profile instead. I knew her posts better than my own timetable. One night I realised I'd read the same page for an hour and remembered nothing, and that scared me a bit. So I did three things. I turned off her notifications and deleted the app from my phone during the week. I told Danish, because I trust him, and asked him to call me out if I brought her up every five minutes. And I threw myself into the robotics project for the inter-school fair. By December I still thought she was nice. But my head was mine again.

qa.q: What project did Asif throw himself into?
qa.a: The robotics project for the inter-school fair.

qa.q: How did Asif feel after reading the same page for an hour?
qa.a: Asif felt a bit scared, realising the thoughts about Arohi were taking over study time.

qa.q: Which of Asif's steps seems most useful, and why?
qa.a: Telling Danish, because a trusted friend can notice and gently call it out when the thoughts start crowding in.

qa.q: How might Danish feel being asked to help?
qa.a: Danish may feel trusted and a little amused, glad to help a friend get focus back.

grounding: A student tells how noticing a crush was crowding out study led to limiting social media, telling a trusted friend and focusing on a project.

passage: I share a hostel room with Zeenat, so I saw how bad it got. In September she was checking Rehan's posts before breakfast, at lunch, under the desk in class. Her notebook had his name in the margins instead of formulas. She failed a Biology test she would normally have topped. One night I heard her talking quietly with Simran, her closest friend, on the corridor bench. I didn't hear all of it, but I heard, "I don't like how much space this takes in my head." The next day her phone went into the warden's box during study hours, and she had deleted the photo app. She signed up for the science exhibition and spent evenings building a water filter model with Simran. I can't say what she felt, but by October the margins of her notebook had equations in them again.

qa.q: What did Zeenat build for the science exhibition?
qa.a: A water filter model, with Simran.

qa.q: What does Zeenat's line about space in her head suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt uneasy and worried about how much the crush was taking over her thoughts.

qa.q: Why did telling Simran help Zeenat?
qa.a: Saying it aloud to a trusted friend made the problem real and brought support, and they worked on the project together.

qa.q: How did the narrator see Zeenat's change by October?
qa.a: The narrator noticed equations filling the notebook margins again, while not being sure exactly what Zeenat felt inside.

grounding: An observer sees a student notice a crush crowding out study, limit phone checking, confide in a friend and refocus on a project.
